A 25% alcohol solution means

Which of the following is hygroscopic in nature?
x: Silica gel absorbs moisture without dissolving; ferric chloride is deliquescent.

q: The component present in lesser amount in a solution is called the ____.
a: solute

q: An example of a liquid-in-solid type solution is ____.
a: mercury in sodium (sodium amalgam)

q: Solubility is the amount of solute dissolved in ____ g of solvent.
Polar compounds are soluble in ____ solvents.
a: polar

q: Volume percentage decreases with increase in temperature because ____.
a: the liquid expands on heating, so the volume of the solution increases

q: Match the following.
Solutions which contain three components are called binary solutions.
x: Solutions with two components are binary; three components make a ternary solution.

q: In a solution, the component which is present in lesser amount is called the solvent.
x: The component in lesser amount is the solute; the one in larger amount is the solvent.

q: Sodium chloride dissolved in water forms a non-aqueous solution.
x: It forms an aqueous solution, because water is the solvent.

q: The molecular formula of green vitriol is MgSO₄·7H₂O.
x: Green vitriol is FeSO₄·7H₂O; MgSO₄·7H₂O is Epsom salt.

q: When silica gel is kept open, it absorbs moisture from the air because it is hygroscopic in nature.
Define the term solution.
a: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances (solute and solvent).

q: What is meant by a binary solution?
a: A solution made of only two components, one solute and one solvent, e.g. salt in water.

q: Give an example each of (i) gas in liquid (ii) solid in liquid (iii) solid in solid (iv) gas in gas.
a: (i) CO₂ in water (soda water) (ii) sugar or salt in water (iii) alloys such as brass (zinc in copper) (iv) air (oxygen in nitrogen).

q: What are aqueous and non-aqueous solutions? Give an example.
a: Aqueous: water is the solvent, e.g. sodium chloride in water. Non-aqueous: a solvent other than water, e.g. sulphur in carbon disulphide.

q: Define volume percentage.
a: The volume of solute in mL present in 100 mL of solution. Volume % = volume of solute ÷ volume of solution × 100.

q: Aquatic animals live more in cold regions. Why?
a: The solubility of oxygen in water is higher at low temperature, so cold water holds more dissolved oxygen.

q: Define hydrated salt.
a: A salt whose crystals contain a fixed number of water molecules (water of crystallisation), e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O.

q: A hot saturated solution of copper sulphate forms crystals as it cools. Why?
a: Solubility of copper sulphate decreases as the temperature falls, so the extra solute that can no longer stay dissolved separates as crystals.

q: Classify into deliquescent and hygroscopic: conc. sulphuric acid, copper sulphate pentahydrate, silica gel, calcium chloride and gypsum salt.
a: Deliquescent: calcium chloride. Hygroscopic: conc. sulphuric acid, silica gel. Copper sulphate pentahydrate and gypsum are hydrated salts (they already contain water of crystallisation); some guides list them as hygroscopic.

q: Write notes on (i) saturated solution (ii) unsaturated solution.
a: (i) Saturated: a solution in which no more solute can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature, e.g. 36 g of NaCl in 100 g of water at 25 °C. (ii) Unsaturated: a solution that contains less solute than it can hold, so more solute can still dissolve, e.g. 10 g of NaCl in 100 g of water at 25 °C.

q: Write notes on the various factors affecting solubility.
a: 1) Nature of solute and solvent: 'like dissolves like', so polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents (NaCl in water) and non-polar in non-polar (grease in petrol). 2) Temperature: for most solids, solubility increases with temperature (endothermic dissolution, e.g. KNO₃); it decreases when dissolution is exothermic (e.g. CaO). Solubility of gases in liquids decreases with temperature. 3) Pressure: affects only gases; by Henry's law the solubility of a gas in a liquid increases with pressure (soda bottles).

q: (a) What happens when MgSO₄·7H₂O is heated? Write the equation. (b) Define solubility.
a: (a) It loses its seven molecules of water of crystallisation and becomes anhydrous magnesium sulphate: MgSO₄·7H₂O → MgSO₄ + 7H₂O. (b) Solubility is the number of grams of solute needed to saturate 100 g of solvent at a given temperature.

q: In what way do hygroscopic substances differ from deliquescent substances?
a: Hygroscopic substances absorb moisture from air but do not dissolve in it, and keep their physical state (e.g. conc. H₂SO₄, silica gel, CaO). Deliquescent substances absorb so much moisture that they dissolve in it and turn into a solution (e.g. NaOH, CaCl₂, FeCl₃).

q: A solution is prepared by dissolving 45 g of sugar in 180 g of water. Calculate the mass percentage of solute.
3.5 litres of ethanol is present in 15 litres of aqueous solution of ethanol. Calculate the volume percent of ethanol.
Vinu dissolves 50 g of sugar in 250 mL of hot water; Sarath dissolves 50 g of the same sugar in 250 mL of cold water. Who gets faster dissolution, and why?
a: Vinu. Sugar dissolves faster in hot water because solubility and the speed of the particles increase with temperature.

q: 'A' is a blue crystalline salt. On heating it loses its blue colour to give 'B'. When water is added, 'B' gives back 'A'. Identify A and B and write the equation.
a: A = copper sulphate pentahydrate CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue vitriol); B = anhydrous copper sulphate CuSO₄ (white). CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O (heat forward, add water back).

q: Will cool drinks give more fizz at the top of the hills or at the foot? Explain.
a: At the top of the hills. Atmospheric pressure is lower there, so less CO₂ stays dissolved (Henry's law) and the gas escapes rapidly when the bottle is opened.
